questions.stem: A 77 year old man with prostate cancer treated with hormone therapy has a 3 week history of band-like pain around his lower chest that is worse when he lies down at night. Today he could not pass urine and his legs feel heavy and stiff. Bladder scan shows 900 mL. There is tenderness over the T9 spinous process.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute urinary retention from prostatic obstruction
Osteoporotic vertebral fracture without cord involvement
questions.e: Severe band-like thoracic pain worse lying down, leg weakness and urinary retention in a man with prostate cancer is metastatic spinal cord compression. Cauda equina syndrome causes low back pain and lower motor neurone signs.

clues: worse when he lies down at night
tenderness over the T9 spinous process
steps.x: Known cancer, night-time band-like thoracic pain, leg weakness and retention.

elim: Would not explain band-like thoracic pain and heavy, stiff legs.
Causes low back pain, saddle anaesthesia and floppy legs, not band-like thoracic pain with stiff legs.
Ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia, without spinal tenderness or a cancer history.
Would not cause urinary retention and leg weakness.

steps.x: D: Metastatic spinal cord compression. Cancer + back pain + neurology + bladder symptoms = MSCC until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer is admitted with 3 days of leg weakness, numbness below the umbilicus and constipation. MRI confirms spinal cord compression at T10. The oncology nurse reviews her history to see what should have prompted earlier referral.
questions.q: Which symptom is most likely to have started first?
questions.e: Back pain, often nocturnal and thoracic, is the most common and earliest symptom of MSCC, often weeks before weakness, sensory loss or sphincter problems; recognising it early prevents paralysis.

steps.x: Established MSCC; the question is about the earliest symptom.

elim: A late autonomic feature of compression.
Comes after pain once the cord is compressed.
A sensory level is a later sign of established compression.
A late sign, often meaning poorer recovery.

steps.x: A: Back pain. Back pain is the most common and earliest symptom; it often precedes neurology by weeks.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with lung cancer has 2 weeks of mid-back pain and 2 days of difficulty walking. MRI is booked and shows compression of the spinal cord at the T10 level. His power in both legs is 3/5.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his legs?
o: Absent ankle reflexes with downgoing plantars
Increased tone with brisk knee reflexes
Normal tone and reflexes with glove-and-stocking sensory loss
Reduced tone with absent knee reflexes
questions.e: Compression of the cord itself, at or above L1, gives upper motor neurone signs below the lesion such as increased tone and brisk reflexes. Absent reflexes and reduced tone suggest a cauda equina (LMN) lesion.

clues: compression of the spinal cord at the T10 level
steps.x: Thoracic cord compression, above L1.

elim: A lower motor neurone pattern, seen in cauda equina syndrome.
Lower motor neurone signs, as in motor neurone disease or chronic root damage.
A peripheral neuropathy pattern.
A lower motor neurone pattern, not cord compression above L1.

steps.x: C: Increased tone with brisk knee reflexes. Cord compression above L1 gives UMN signs below the lesion: spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars, sensory level.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with myeloma has 1 week of low back pain, numbness around his anus and difficulty passing urine. Examination shows mild weakness of both legs, absent ankle reflexes and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Knee reflexes are brisk. MRI shows a vertebral lesion at the T12/L1 level.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Compression of the conus medullaris at about L1 gives a mixed picture: absent ankle jerks (LMN) with extensor plantars (UMN) and early sphincter problems. Cauda equina syndrome gives purely LMN signs.

steps.x: A mixed UMN and LMN picture at the T12/L1 level.

elim: Pure lower motor neurone signs; plantars would be downgoing.
Causes claudication-type leg pain on walking, not sphincter problems with mixed signs.
Would not cause extensor plantars or sphincter problems.
Gives pure upper motor neurone signs with brisk ankle jerks.

steps.x: B: Conus medullaris syndrome. Conus (around L1): mixed UMN and LMN signs, e.g. absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has 3 days of low back pain shooting down the back of his right leg to the sole of his foot, after lifting a heavy box. He has numbness of the lateral border of his right foot and a reduced right ankle reflex. Bladder and bowel function are normal and perianal sensation is intact.
questions.q: At which level is the disc herniation most likely?
questions.e: Acute unilateral pain and numbness after lifting is typical of disc herniation, most often at L5/S1; S1 root compression causes lateral foot numbness and a reduced ankle reflex. Intact perianal sensation and sphincters make cauda equina syndrome unlikely.

clues: lateral border of his right foot
steps.x: Unilateral S1 root signs with no sphincter involvement.

elim: Affects the thigh and knee reflex, not the sole and ankle reflex.
Gives anterior thigh pain and a reduced knee reflex.
Usually compresses L5, giving dorsum of foot numbness and weak big toe extension with a normal ankle reflex.
Would affect the conus, with sphincter involvement and mixed signs.

steps.x: D: L5/S1. Most disc herniations are at L5/S1, compressing the S1 root: lateral foot numbness, reduced ankle jerk.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has 6 weeks of haemoptysis and 8 kg weight loss. He has smoked for 50 years. For 2 weeks he has had severe mid-thoracic back pain at night, and today he has weak legs and a sensory level at T6. MRI shows a destructive lesion of the T6 vertebral body compressing the cord.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Metastatic cord compression most commonly comes from prostate, breast, lung or myeloma, spreading to the vertebral body; haemoptysis and weight loss in a heavy smoker point to lung cancer. TB usually involves the disc space.

clues: destructive lesion of the T6 vertebral body
steps.x: Smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss plus a vertebral body lesion compressing the cord.

elim: No fever or risk factors for infection, with clear features of lung cancer.
Would not explain haemoptysis and weight loss.
Rare, and does not cause a destructive vertebral body lesion.
Usually affects the disc space and two adjacent vertebrae with fever and night sweats.

steps.x: B: Metastasis from lung cancer. MSCC is most often from prostate, breast, lung or myeloma; lung fits here.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with prostate cancer sees his GP with 10 days of severe pain in his upper back. It is constant, keeps him awake at night and is getting worse despite paracetamol and codeine. There is tenderness over the T4 spinous process. Neurological examination of his legs is normal and he passes urine normally.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Spinal metastasis threatening the spinal cord
questions.e: Severe, progressive thoracic pain that disturbs sleep with localised spinal tenderness are red flags for spinal metastasis and impending MSCC in a patient with cancer, even before neurological signs (NICE CG75).

clues: tenderness over the T4 spinous process
Neurological examination of his legs is normal
steps.x: Red-flag thoracic pain in a cancer patient, no neurology yet.

elim: Does not cause unremitting night pain with focal spinal tenderness in a cancer patient.
A diagnosis of exclusion; red flags here point to metastasis.
Causes bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, not focal thoracic spinal tenderness.
Rare and would not explain red-flag night pain in a man with prostate cancer.

steps.x: D: Spinal metastasis threatening the spinal cord. Cancer + severe thoracic pain disturbing sleep + spinal tenderness = spinal metastasis threatening the cord, even before neurology.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman had a knee replacement under spinal anaesthesia with an epidural catheter for pain relief. She is on enoxaparin. Twelve hours after the catheter is removed she develops severe back pain and then numbness and weakness of both legs over 2 hours. Her BP is 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Spinal epidural haematoma is linked to anticoagulation and iatrogenic dural puncture such as epidural analgesia; bleeding into the closed spinal canal rapidly compresses the cord. An abscess develops over days with fever.

clues: weakness of both legs over 2 hours
steps.x: Dural puncture plus anticoagulation, then sudden back pain and rapid leg weakness.

elim: Sudden onset, sparing dorsal column sensation, without a link to dural puncture.
Develops over days with fever, not hours after catheter removal.
Develops over days to weeks after infection, without back pain at a puncture site.
Gives a postural headache, not leg weakness.

steps.x: E: Spinal epidural haematoma. Epidural haematoma: anticoagulation or dural puncture (e.g. epidural analgesia) with rapid compression.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has taken prednisolone for 10 years for polymyalgia rheumatica. She felt a sudden severe pain in her mid-back while lifting a shopping bag. Over the next 3 days her legs have become weak and she has a sensory level at T11. She has no history of cancer and her calcium, ESR and serum protein electrophoresis are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her cord compression?
questions.e: Vertebral collapse is a recognised cause of spinal cord compression; long-term steroids cause osteoporosis, and a fracture after minor strain can retropulse bone into the canal. There is no cancer history to suggest metastasis.

steps.x: Long-term steroids, sudden pain with minor strain, then cord signs.

elim: No fever or infection risk factors, and the onset was sudden with lifting.
Would cause root signs in the leg, not a thoracic sensory level.
No known cancer and normal screening bloods; the history points to fracture.
Not anticoagulated and no dural puncture.

steps.x: D: Osteoporotic vertebral collapse. Vertebral collapse is a cause of cord compression; long-term steroids cause osteoporosis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with breast cancer has thoracic back pain and walks with a stiff, scissoring gait. Her right plantar response is extensor (positive Babinski sign) and both knee reflexes are brisk. She has reduced perianal sensation.
questions.q: Where is the lesion most likely to be?
questions.e: A positive Babinski sign with perianal sensory loss suggests cord compression at a higher level, often from metastatic disease, because the cord carries fibres for all lower segments. Cauda equina lesions give LMN signs.

steps.x: UMN signs plus perianal sensory loss in a cancer patient.

elim: Gives lower motor neurone signs, with downgoing plantars and reduced reflexes.
Gives unilateral foot drop with dermatomal sensory loss, not brisk reflexes.
Would not cause perianal sensory loss and thoracic pain, and usually affects one side.
Give reduced reflexes and distal sensory loss.

steps.x: E: Thoracic spinal cord. A positive Babinski with perianal sensory loss suggests compression at a higher (cord) level, often metastatic.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has 1 day of severe low back pain with pain down both legs. She has not passed urine since the morning and feels numb 'down below' when she wipes after using the toilet. Her leg power is 4/5 with reduced ankle reflexes. A bladder scan shows 750 mL.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on further examination?
questions.e: Cauda equina syndrome is a lower motor neurone root pattern: saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, reduced anal tone and bilateral sciatica. Brisk reflexes and extensor plantars point to the cord itself.

steps.x: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia and retention: cauda equina syndrome.

elim: An upper motor neurone sign, not expected with root compression.
An upper motor neurone sign of cord compression.
Spasticity is upper motor neurone; cauda equina causes reduced tone.
Indicates thoracic cord compression at T10.

steps.x: D: Reduced anal tone. Cauda equina: LMN/root pattern with saddle anaesthesia, retention and reduced anal tone.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer had 5 weeks of night-time thoracic back pain before he presented with complete paralysis of both legs and urinary retention. MRI showed compression at T8. He received dexamethasone and radiotherapy. Three months later he has no recovery of leg power.
questions.q: Which other long-term problem is he most likely to have?
o: Lower motor neurone weakness of the arms
questions.e: Delay allows permanent damage: paralysis, loss of mobility, chronic neuropathic pain, sexual dysfunction and permanent bladder and bowel dysfunction. A T8 lesion does not affect the arms.

clues: 5 weeks of night-time thoracic back pain
steps.x: Delayed diagnosis with complete paralysis and sphincter involvement.

elim: Can occur with bone metastases but is not a consequence of the compression itself.
A T8 lesion spares the arms.
Not caused by spinal cord compression.
Steroids cause hyperglycaemia, not diabetes insipidus.

steps.x: C: Permanent bladder dysfunction. Late MSCC causes permanent paralysis and sphincter dysfunction; function at presentation predicts outcome.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with metastatic lung cancer arrives in the Emergency Department at 11 pm with 1 week of thoracic back pain and 1 day of leg weakness. Her MRI is booked for the morning. She has no history of peptic ulcer disease and her capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate action before the MRI?
o: Wait for MRI before giving any treatment
questions.e: In suspected malignant cord compression, dexamethasone 16 mg is given immediately, before the MRI, to reduce cord oedema. Waiting for imaging risks irreversible damage.

clues: MRI is booked for the morning
steps.x: Suspected MSCC with neurology; imaging is hours away.

elim: Does not assess the cord and delays treatment.
Treats hypercalcaemia or bone pain; it does not treat cord oedema.
Not indicated and could worsen a spinal block.
Steroids should start before imaging if MSCC is suspected.

steps.x: B: Give dexamethasone 16 mg. Give dexamethasone first, before investigations, if MSCC is suspected.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer has 1 week of back pain and new weakness of both legs. Examination shows a sensory level at T10 and brisk knee reflexes. A bone scan last year showed metastases in the thoracic and lumbar spine and pelvis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
MRI of the thoracic spine only
Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine
questions.e: MRI of the whole spine within 24 hours is first-line in suspected MSCC (NICE CG75), because compression is often at more than one level. Imaging only the thoracic spine may miss a second site.

steps.x: Suspected MSCC with multilevel spinal metastases.

elim: Stages cancer but does not show the cord well.
May miss compression at other levels; metastases are often multilevel.
Cannot show cord compression.
Shows bone metastases but not the cord or epidural space.

steps.x: C: MRI of the whole spine. MRI whole spine within 24 hours: metastases are often at several levels.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has 6 days of severe thoracic back pain and fever. Today his legs are weak. His temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 112 bpm. MRI shows a thoracic epidural collection compressing the cord. He has not yet had antibiotics.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to identify the cause?
questions.e: Epidural abscess presents with fever, back pain and a neurological deficit in people with infection risks such as diabetes; blood cultures identify the organism, often Staphylococcus aureus, before antibiotics start.

steps.x: Fever, back pain and neuro deficit with an epidural collection: abscess.

elim: For metastatic prostate cancer, not an infected collection.
For myeloma, not infection.
For gout, not relevant here.
For myeloma, not infection.

steps.x: A: Blood cultures. Epidural abscess: take blood cultures (often Staphylococcus aureus) before antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has 2 months of back pain and tiredness and 2 days of leg weakness with a sensory level at T9. She has no known cancer. MRI shows multiple lytic vertebral lesions with cord compression at T9.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to identify the underlying cause?
o: Serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains
questions.e: Myeloma is one of the commonest causes of MSCC; hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and lytic lesions point to it, confirmed with serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains.

steps.x: Lytic lesions, anaemia, high calcium and renal impairment: myeloma.

elim: For connective tissue disease, not lytic lesions.
A colorectal marker; does not explain this blood picture.
For ankylosing spondylitis, not lytic lesions with anaemia and renal impairment.
Does not explain lytic lesions with hypercalcaemia and renal impairment.

steps.x: D: Serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains. Myeloma is a common cause of MSCC; confirm with serum electrophoresis and free light chains.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has 2 days of severe low back pain and pain down both legs after a gym session. This evening she noticed numbness of her buttocks and inner thighs and has not passed urine for 10 hours. Her leg power is 4/5. Bladder scan shows 800 mL.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
questions.e: Suspected cauda equina compression needs emergency MRI of the spine and referral to the spinal or neurosurgical team; delay risks permanent sphincter loss.

clues: numbness of her buttocks and inner thighs
steps.x: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia and retention: cauda equina syndrome.

elim: Does not show nerve root compression well.
Slow and not the test for compression.
Too slow; this is an emergency.
Cannot show disc or root compression.

steps.x: B: Emergency MRI of the spine. Suspected compression with sphincter involvement: emergency MRI, then neurosurgery.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with renal cell carcinoma has 2 weeks of thoracic back pain at night and new unsteadiness. His legs are stiff with brisk reflexes and he has a sensory level at T5. MRI of the whole spine is performed within 24 hours.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI?
o: Demyelinating plaques in the cervical cord
Vertebral body metastasis extending into the epidural space
questions.e: Metastatic cord compression most often arises from a vertebral body metastasis that extends into the epidural space and compresses the cord by direct pressure and venous congestion.

steps.x: Cancer, night pain, UMN signs and a sensory level: MSCC.

elim: Below the cord and would not cause a T5 sensory level.
Seen in multiple sclerosis without back pain and cancer.
Causes dissociated sensory loss in a cape distribution, not cancer-related pain.
Would not fit UMN signs with a sensory level.

steps.x: E: Vertebral body metastasis extending into the epidural space. MSCC usually arises from vertebral body metastases growing back into the epidural space.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has suspected spinal cord compression at T7. She was given dexamethasone 16 mg orally in the Emergency Department this morning. MRI is planned and she is waiting to see the spinal team. The ward doctor writes her regular drug chart.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate regular prescription?
o: Dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily with a proton pump inhibitor
Prednisolone 5 mg once daily with a proton pump inhibitor
questions.e: After a 16 mg stat dose, dexamethasone is continued at 8 mg twice daily with a proton pump inhibitor to prevent steroid-induced peptic ulceration while awaiting definitive treatment.

steps.x: Stat dose given; maintenance and gastric protection needed.

elim: Far above the recommended maintenance dose.
Too low a dose, and no gastric protection.
Used for adrenal crisis, not cord oedema.
Too low a dose and not the recommended steroid.

steps.x: C: Dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily with a proton pump inhibitor. Dexamethasone 16 mg stat, then 8 mg BD, plus a PPI for steroid ulcer prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man with renal cell carcinoma is otherwise well and walks his dog daily. He has 2 days of leg weakness. MRI shows a single-level metastasis at T9 compressing the cord, with an unstable vertebra. His expected survival is more than a year. He has been given dexamethasone.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Surgical decompression, after stabilisation with steroids, is definitive treatment for a fit patient with single-level MSCC and an unstable spine. Steroids alone reduce oedema but do not relieve compression.

steps.x: Fit patient, single level, unstable spine, good prognosis.

elim: Leaves the cord compressed and spine unstable.
Too slow to relieve compression.
Steroids only stabilise; they do not decompress.
He is fit with a good prognosis.

steps.x: E: Surgical decompression and stabilisation. Gold standard: surgical decompression after stabilisation with steroids; delay causes irreversible injury.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer to multiple vertebrae has MRI-confirmed cord compression at T6 and T11. She is bed-bound from frailty and her oncologist estimates her prognosis at a few months. The spinal surgeons say she is not fit for surgery. She is on dexamethasone.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Radiotherapy is used when the patient cannot have surgery, for example with multilevel disease, frailty or short prognosis. Surgery is the definitive option only for those fit enough.

steps.x: Multilevel MSCC in a patient unable to have surgery.

elim: She is unfit for surgery.
Radiotherapy can reduce pain and preserve function.
For chronic neuropathic pain, not compression.
Treats painful fractures, not epidural compression.

steps.x: C: Radiotherapy. Radiotherapy if the patient cannot undergo surgery.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man with prostate cancer has 4 days of thoracic back pain and new leg weakness. He has been given dexamethasone 16 mg. Whole-spine MRI confirms cord compression at T10 from a vertebral metastasis.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase his hormone therapy and review in 2 weeks
Urgent referral to the acute oncology and spinal surgical teams
questions.e: Confirmed MSCC needs urgent referral to acute oncology and neurosurgery or spinal surgery the same day, to decide between surgery and radiotherapy. Delay risks permanent paralysis.

steps.x: MSCC confirmed on MRI.

elim: Unsafe; MSCC is an emergency.
Too slow to relieve compression.
Not indicated and does not treat compression.
Mobilising an unstable spine before a plan is unsafe.

steps.x: E: Urgent referral to the acute oncology and spinal surgical teams. After MRI: urgent referral to acute oncology/neurosurgery with escalation to seniors.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man who injects drugs has 5 days of thoracic back pain and fever, and today has weakness of both legs. His temperature is 39.2°C. MRI shows a thoracic epidural abscess compressing the cord. Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Intravenous antibiotics and urgent surgical drainage
Oral antibiotics and review in 1 week
Paracetamol and repeat MRI in 48 hours
Wait for culture results before antibiotics
questions.e: An epidural abscess with neurological deficit needs urgent IV antibiotics and surgical drainage. Steroids and radiotherapy are for malignant compression.

steps.x: IVDU with fever, back pain, neuro deficit: epidural abscess.

elim: For malignant compression, not infection.
Inadequate for an abscess compressing the cord.
Leaves the cord compressed and infection untreated.
Delays treatment of a time-critical infection.

steps.x: B: Intravenous antibiotics and urgent surgical drainage. Treat the cause: abscess = urgent IV antibiotics plus surgical drainage.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 1 day of bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention after lifting a wardrobe. Emergency MRI shows a large central L4/L5 disc prolapse compressing the cauda equina. She has no history of cancer.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Cauda equina syndrome from a central disc prolapse needs urgent surgical decompression to save bladder, bowel and sexual function. Dexamethasone and radiotherapy are for malignant compression.

steps.x: Cauda equina syndrome from a disc.

elim: Leaves the roots compressed; risks permanent sphincter loss.
For malignant compression, not disc prolapse.
For radicular pain, not cauda equina syndrome.
Too slow for an emergency.

steps.x: E: Urgent surgical decompression. Disc prolapse causing cauda equina syndrome: urgent surgical decompression.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with atrial fibrillation takes warfarin. He develops sudden severe interscapular back pain followed within 3 hours by weakness of both legs. His INR is 5.8. MRI shows an epidural haematoma compressing the thoracic cord.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Reverse anticoagulation and urgent surgical evacuation
Stop warfarin and review in 1 week
Withhold one dose of warfarin and continue
questions.e: A spinal epidural haematoma is a neurosurgical emergency: anticoagulation is reversed (vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin) and the haematoma is evacuated surgically.

steps.x: Anticoagulated man with rapid cord compression from a bleed.

elim: For malignant compression, not haematoma.
For abscess, not haematoma.
Too slow; the cord is compressed now.
Leaves him anticoagulated and the cord compressed.

steps.x: C: Reverse anticoagulation and urgent surgical evacuation. Epidural haematoma: a neurosurgical emergency; reverse anticoagulation and evacuate.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with breast cancer phones the oncology helpline. She has had 1 week of severe thoracic back pain that wakes her at night and, since this morning, her legs have felt weak and she has stumbled twice. She has no fever.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise heat packs and review with her GP next week
Increase her analgesia and review in 2 weeks
Same-day assessment with urgent MRI of the whole spine
questions.e: Thoracic pain disturbing sleep with new leg weakness in a patient with cancer are red flags for MSCC; she needs urgent same-day assessment, dexamethasone and whole-spine MRI within 24 hours (NICE CG75).

steps.x: Red-flag pain plus new neurology in a cancer patient.

elim: Ignores red flags for MSCC.
Too slow and does not show the cord.
Delays an emergency.
Inappropriate with progressive neurology.

steps.x: E: Same-day assessment with urgent MRI of the whole spine. Red flags + neurology = same-day referral, dexamethasone and MRI within 24 hours.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has MRI-confirmed compression of the spinal cord at T6 from a metastasis. His leg reflexes are brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. A student asks why his reflexes are increased rather than reduced.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Compression of the dorsal root ganglia
Damage to anterior horn cells of the legs
Increased sensory input from the legs
Loss of descending inhibition from the corticospinal tracts
questions.e: Compression above the conus damages corticospinal tract fibres destined for lower segments, removing descending inhibition, so the reflex arcs below become brisk with extensor plantars.

clues: compression of the spinal cord at T6
steps.x: Thoracic cord lesion with UMN signs.

elim: Would cause sensory loss and reduced reflexes.
A lower motor neurone lesion, giving reduced reflexes.
Not the mechanism of hyperreflexia.
A lower motor neurone lesion with reduced reflexes.

steps.x: D: Loss of descending inhibition from the corticospinal tracts. Above the conus, the compressed cord carries corticospinal fibres for lower levels; loss of their inhibition gives UMN signs.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has MRI-confirmed compression at the L3 vertebral level. His legs are weak and floppy, his knee and ankle reflexes are absent, and both plantar responses are downgoing. A student expected upper motor neurone signs because the spine is compressed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his signs?
o: The spinal cord ends above L3, so nerve roots are compressed
questions.e: The cord ends at the conus medullaris around L1; compression below this affects lumbosacral nerve roots (peripheral nerves), giving LMN signs such as flaccid weakness and reduced reflexes.

steps.x: Compression below L1 with LMN signs.

elim: Spinal shock follows acute cord injury; it does not explain this chronic pattern at L3.
Would give UMN signs.
Does not explain the pattern at a single level.
Would give UMN signs.

steps.x: E: The spinal cord ends above L3, so nerve roots are compressed. The cord ends at the conus (about L1); below that are the cauda equina roots, which are peripheral nerves.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with prostate cancer has 2 days of leg weakness from MRI-confirmed cord compression. Within 24 hours of starting dexamethasone his leg power improves from 3/5 to 4/5, before any radiotherapy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the early improvement?
o: Increased bone density of the vertebra
Reduction of vasogenic oedema in the cord
questions.e: Tumour compression causes venous congestion, oedema and direct pressure; dexamethasone quickly reduces the reversible vasogenic oedema, which is why it is given immediately in suspected MSCC.

steps.x: Fast improvement with steroids alone.

elim: Steroids do not kill most solid tumours within a day; radiotherapy does this.
Takes months and does not decompress the cord.
Does not happen within a day.
Steroids suppress, not treat, infection; this is not infection.

steps.x: C: Reduction of vasogenic oedema in the cord. Compression causes venous congestion and oedema; early oedema is reversible with steroids.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with prostate cancer is found to have metastases in his thoracic and lumbar vertebral bodies but not in his lungs or liver. A student asks how the tumour reached the spine.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of spread?
o: Direct invasion along the spinal nerves
Haematogenous spread through the valveless vertebral venous plexus
Lymphatic spread through the thoracic duct
questions.e: MSCC usually starts from vertebral body metastases (prostate, breast, lung, myeloma); prostate cancer reaches the spine through the valveless vertebral venous (Batson's) plexus, bypassing the lungs and liver.

clues: not in his lungs or liver
steps.x: Spine metastases without lung or liver disease.

elim: Not the usual route from prostate to vertebral body.
Not the main route to vertebral bodies.
Causes leptomeningeal disease, not vertebral body metastases.
Leads to liver metastases.

steps.x: B: Haematogenous spread through the valveless vertebral venous plexus. Prostate venous blood reaches the vertebrae via the valveless Batson's plexus; MSCC usually starts in the vertebral body.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman on apixaban has an epidural catheter placed for abdominal surgery. Four hours later she has sudden back pain and becomes unable to move her legs over 90 minutes. MRI shows a blood collection in the epidural space.
questions.q: Which best explains why her deficit developed so fast?
o: Bleeding raises pressure quickly within the closed spinal canal
questions.e: Bleeding into the epidural space, often linked to anticoagulation or dural puncture, rapidly raises pressure in the closed spinal canal, compressing the cord within hours; this makes it a neurosurgical emergency.

clues: blood collection in the epidural space
steps.x: Anticoagulation plus dural puncture, then rapid deficit.

elim: Develops over days to weeks.
Develops over days with fever.
Causes a temporary block, and would not be seen on MRI as a collection.
Not caused by catheter placement.

steps.x: B: Bleeding raises pressure quickly within the closed spinal canal. The spinal canal is a closed space; blood rapidly raises pressure and compresses the cord.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with prostate cancer was walking at diagnosis of cord compression and received treatment within 24 hours; he still walks. His neighbour, with the same cancer, waited 10 days with leg weakness before seeking help and remains paralysed despite treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for the difference in outcome?
o: Delay allowed irreversible ischaemic injury to the cord
The neighbour had a peripheral neuropathy
questions.e: Cord compression is time-critical: delay in decompression allows ischaemic injury to the cord and roots, which is irreversible. Ability to walk at the start of treatment best predicts walking afterwards.

steps.x: Same disease, different delays.

steps.x: A: Delay allowed irreversible ischaemic injury to the cord. Delay lets compression cause ischaemic cord damage, which does not recover: treat as time-critical.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has cauda equina syndrome from a large L5/S1 disc prolapse. She has saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, reduced anal tone and absent ankle reflexes. Her plantar responses are downgoing and her leg tone is reduced.
questions.q: Which structures are most likely to be compressed?
o: Anterior horn cells in the thoracic cord
Corticospinal tracts in the thoracic cord
Dorsal columns in the cervical cord
Lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris
questions.e: Cauda equina syndrome compresses the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris; these are peripheral nerves, so the signs are LMN: flaccid weakness, reduced reflexes and saddle anaesthesia.

steps.x: Low disc with pure LMN signs and sphincter loss.

elim: Would not give saddle anaesthesia from a disc at L5/S1.
Would give UMN signs.
Would affect the arms and give UMN signs.
Would not explain absent ankle reflexes.

steps.x: D: Lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris. Cauda equina = compressed lumbosacral roots (peripheral nerves) below the conus, so LMN signs.
